title: Restitution of Conjugal Rights — Section 9 HMA

content.overview: Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 allows the aggrieved spouse to petition for restitution of conjugal rights where the other has withdrawn from society without reasonable excuse. The burden of proving reasonable excuse lies on the person who withdrew. Non-compliance for one year or more is a ground for divorce under s. 13(1A). Constitutional validity was upheld in Saroj Rani.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Valid marriage? (2) Withdrawal from society? (3) Without reasonable excuse? (4) Legal ground to refuse? (5) Non-compliance pathway to s. 13(1A)?
content.study:
When either spouse has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may petition for restitution of conjugal rights. The Court may decree restitution if satisfied of the truth of the petition and that there is no legal ground why it should not be granted.

Explanation: burden of proving reasonable excuse is on the person who has withdrawn.

The decree does not authorise physical detention or forced sexual relations. Practical significance often lies in the pathway to divorce under s. 13(1A) after non-resumption of cohabitation for one year or more.

Saroj Rani upheld constitutional validity; courts apply the section with a rights-sensitive approach and refuse where cohabitation would be unjust or unsafe.

Case-law verification remains a separate gate.

sections.heading: Ingredients
sections.body: Valid marriage; withdrawal from society; without reasonable excuse; no legal ground against the decree.

sections.heading: Burden of reasonable excuse
sections.body: Once withdrawal is shown, the Explanation places the burden of proving reasonable excuse on the respondent.

sections.heading: Nature of the decree
sections.body: Aims at restoration of marital companionship; does not compel sexual intercourse or physical detention.

sections.heading: Pathway to divorce
sections.body: Non-resumption of cohabitation for one year or more after the decree → s. 13(1A) divorce ground for either party.

sections.heading: Constitutional context
sections.body: Validity upheld in Saroj Rani; residual discretion to refuse where cohabitation would be unjust.

examples.title: Restitution granted
examples.body: Spouse leaves without alleging cruelty or other excuse — restitution may be granted if no legal ground against it.

examples.title: Reasonable excuse
examples.body: Respondent proves continuous cruelty — withdrawal with reasonable excuse; petition fails.

hypotheticals.question: After a restitution decree, cohabitation is not resumed for over a year. Is divorce available?
hypotheticals.analysis: Yes under s. 13(1A) for either party, subject to the ordinary requirements of that provision.

distinctions.title: Restitution (s. 9) vs Judicial Separation (s. 10)
distinctions.left: Restore cohabitation; ground is withdrawal without reasonable excuse.
distinctions.right: Relieve duty to cohabit; grounds track s. 13 divorce grounds.

misconceptions.trap: A restitution decree forces physical cohabitation or sexual relations.
misconceptions.correction: It does not authorise detention or forced sexual relations; practical effect often is the s. 13(1A) pathway.

misconceptions.trap: Section 9 is unconstitutional after recognition of privacy.
misconceptions.correction: Saroj Rani upheld validity; courts refuse the decree where cohabitation would be unjust.

cases.name: Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha
cases.facts: Constitutional challenge to s. 9 on privacy and personal liberty grounds.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Section 9 is constitutionally valid. The decree aims at restoration of marital companionship and does not compel sexual intercourse.
cases.relevance: Binding orientation on constitutionality; verification open.
